extracted.intended_audience: princes, rulers, and statesmen (political leaders seeking practical advice on acquiring and holding states)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical prescriptions for acquiring and retaining control of principalities (cities, regions, or kingdoms), including how to treat former ruling families, whether to reside there, use colonies or garrisons, handle neighbouring powers, and manage newly founded or fortune-made princedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destroy the family of the former prince
rubrics_metrics.description: “to hold them securely it is enough to have destroyed the family of the prince who was ruling them”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate the former ruler's family to remove rival claimants and dynastic focal points for rebellion. This is presented as one of two essential considerations when annexing a state that had a previous prince; without the family there is little remaining authority to rally opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep their laws and taxes unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: “neither their laws nor their taxes are altered”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve existing legal and fiscal arrangements so that the annexed population retains continuity and can more easily become ‘one body’ with the conquering principality. Machiavelli cites examples (Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, Normandy) where similarity of customs and unchanged institutions aided peaceful incorporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reside personally in culturally different territories
rubrics_metrics.description: “he who has acquired them should go and reside there”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For territories differing in language, customs, or laws, the prince should live there to perceive and remedy disorders early, prevent official pillage, provide prompt justice, and deter outside attack. Example: the Turk’s residence in Greece made holding that territory possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send colonies as keys to occupied territories
rubrics_metrics.description: “The other and better course is to send colonies to one or two places, which may be as keys to that state”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish colonies in strategic points rather than relying solely on a large standing garrison. Colonies are relatively cheap, faithful, injure fewer people, and offend only a small dispossessed minority who remain weak and scattered; they provide durable control without exhausting the state's income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer colonies to garrisons (avoid costly standing troops)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince who maintains armed men (garrisons) spends much more and may consume all the income from the state; colonies are cheaper and less provocative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garrisons impose heavy burdens, cause hardship through their movements, make the entire population hostile, and can turn the acquisition into a loss. Colonies generally produce less resistance and are more useful than stationary garrisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either treat people well or crush them
rubrics_metrics.description: “men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves of lighter injuries, of more serious ones they cannot”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid half-measures: small injuries leave enemies capable of revenge; very severe punishment (so extreme that revenge is impossible) prevents later reprisals. When inflicting injury, make it such that one need not live in fear of vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as head/defender of weaker neighbours and weaken stronger ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should make himself the head and defender of his less powerful neighbours, and weaken the more powerful amongst them
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep smaller states friendly (without giving them too much power) and curb the ambitions of larger neighbours so no foreign power as strong as yourself can gain a foothold. Use local goodwill and your own forces to keep dominant neighbours in check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent powerful foreigners from gaining footholds
rubrics_metrics.description: “take care that no foreigner as powerful as himself shall, by any accident, get a footing there”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary that discontented factions may invite an external power; ensure no outside potentate can be introduced who will attract subject states to his side. The Romans’ conduct in Greece is given as a model—deny powerful outsiders influence and keep smaller allies weak enough to need you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresee troubles and remedy them early
rubrics_metrics.description: When evils are foreseen they can be quickly redressed; if you wait until they approach, the remedy is too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act proactively: correct dangers while small (physician/hectic fever analogy). Delay only benefits others; do not attempt to avoid inevitable conflict by short-term concessions that worsen long-term position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not enable or aggrandise another power who will later threaten you
rubrics_metrics.description: “he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid actions that increase the strength or authority of another power (e.g., aggrandizing the Church or Spain in Italy) because the beneficiary will become a danger. The examples of Louis XII show the danger of enriching other powers and thereby undermining oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different approaches required for states governed by servants vs. by barons
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of governments: one by a prince with servants (whose offices depend on the prince), the other by prince and barons (lords with hereditary authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States governed by prince-and-servants are hard to seize but easy to hold once conquered (no one is recognized superior); those with established barons are easy to enter through malcontent nobles but very hard to hold because the barons can become rallying leaders of resistance. Policies for acquisition and retention must differ accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: For cities used to freedom: ruin, reside, or establish a prince-created oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Three courses: ruin them; reside there in person; or permit them to live under their own laws while establishing an oligarchy friendly to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities accustomed to freedom retain the rallying cry of liberty and, unless disunited or dispersed, will rebel; thus the safest methods are destruction/dismantling or residence. Establishing an oligarchy created by the prince can succeed (it depends on making that oligarchy reliant on the prince). Examples: Romans dismantled Capua/Numantia; Spartans’ attempt to rule Greek cities as free failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities accustomed to a prince are easier to hold
rubrics_metrics.description: When cities/countries are accustomed to live under a prince and his family is exterminated, they cannot form a new ruler and are slow to take up arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such populations lack experience self-governing and are therefore more readily secured by a prince who gains their goodwill or governs effectively; contrast with republics where vitality and desire for vengeance make them dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: New princes must rely on their own arms (armed prophets succeed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If innovators must use prayers they always succeed badly; but when they can rely on themselves and use force, then they are rarely endangered—'all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men who create new orders face enemies who benefited under the old and lukewarm supporters among potential beneficiaries; without their own loyal armed force they cannot enforce institutions. Examples: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus (armed and succeeded) vs. Savonarola (unarmed and destroyed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Those raised by fortune must promptly lay foundations after ascent
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who unexpectedly become princes must be prepared at once to hold what fortune has thrown into their laps by laying the necessary foundations afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on the favour of others leaves one unstable; a fortune-made prince must quickly secure loyal forces, institutions, and alliances to convert rapid rise into durable rule. Examples: contrast Francesco Sforza (laid foundations, kept power) and Cesare Borgia (lost power when fortune declined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calculated cruelty through agents, then publicly disavow it
rubrics_metrics.description: The duke promoted a swift and cruel governor (Ramiro d’Orco) to restore order, then executed him publicly and displayed the instruments of cruelty to show the prince was not personally barbarous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint a severe enforcer to restore order where necessary, then remove and punish that enforcer in public to reassure the populace and dissociate the prince from the cruelty while preserving the order achieved. This tactic transforms necessary severity into popular satisfaction and fear without permanently branding the prince as brutal.
